patient.chief_complaint: Progressive headache, left arm weakness, and a witnessed seizure
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Diego Ramirez is a 52-year-old right-handed man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home this morning. His wife reports that over the past three to four weeks, he has been complaining of progressively worsening headaches, predominantly on the right side, that are worst in the early morning and sometimes wake him from sleep. She notes that the headaches are unlike any he has experienced before and are associated with nausea and occasional vomiting. Over the past two weeks, she has also noticed that he has been clumsier with his left hand, dropping things more frequently, and that his left arm seems weaker than usual. He has also had increasing difficulty finding the right words during conversations, which is very uncharacteristic for him as a teacher. His colleagues at work have remarked that he seems less organized and occasionally forgetful over the past month. This morning at approximately 7:15 AM, while eating breakfast, he suddenly stopped speaking, his eyes deviated to the right, and he developed rhythmic jerking of the left arm that rapidly generalized to a full tonic-clonic convulsion lasting approximately 90 seconds. He was postictal and confused for about 20 minutes before EMS arrived. He had never had a seizure before. In the emergency department, a non-contrast CT of the head was obtained and demonstrated a large right frontal mass with surrounding edema and approximately 8 mm of left-to-right midline shift. He was started on levetiracetam and dexamethasone. He has been admitted to the neurosurgery service for further workup and management.

results.title: Radiotherapy plus concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide for glioblastoma
results.authors: Stupp R, Mason WP, van den Bent MJ, et al.
results.summary: Landmark RCT demonstrating that adding temozolomide to radiotherapy improved median survival from 12.1 to 14.6 months and 2-year survival from 10% to 27% in glioblastoma patients.

results.title: Effects of radiotherapy with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide versus radiotherapy alone on survival in glioblastoma: long-term follow-up of the EORTC/NCIC trial
results.authors: Stupp R, Hegi ME, Mason WP, et al.
results.summary: Long-term follow-up of the Stupp trial showing 5-year overall survival of 9.8% with temozolomide vs 1.9% with radiotherapy alone. MGMT methylation was the strongest predictor of benefit.

results.title: MGMT gene silencing and benefit from temozolomide in glioblastoma
results.authors: Hegi ME, Diserens AC, Gorlia T, et al.
results.summary: MGMT promoter methylation status predicts benefit from temozolomide. Methylated patients had significantly better outcomes. Unmethylated patients derived less benefit but the Stupp protocol remains standard of care.

output.summary: The standard of care for newly diagnosed glioblastoma is the Stupp protocol: maximal safe surgical resection followed by concurrent temozolomide (75 mg/m2 daily) with focal radiotherapy (60 Gy in 30 fractions over 6 weeks), then adjuvant temozolomide (150-200 mg/m2 for 5 days every 28 days, 6-12 cycles). MGMT promoter methylation is the strongest molecular predictor of temozolomide response. For MGMT-unmethylated tumors, the protocol remains standard, though benefit is reduced. Tumor Treating Fields (TTFields) can be added to adjuvant temozolomide based on the EF-14 trial. For elderly patients (>70 years), abbreviated radiation with or without temozolomide is an option.

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiogram has no role in the diagnostic workup of suspected high-grade glioma absent a specific cardiac question (e.g., suspected paraneoplastic endocarditis)
Cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of a brain mass and adds resource cost without informing management

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in suspected intracranial mass with imaging evidence of herniation: the pressure gradient created by LP risks transtentorial or tonsillar herniation. Even when LP is otherwise safe, CSF studies are low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede any lumbar puncture when a mass lesion is suspected, to identify mass effect and herniation risk before LP
Adequate pre-operative MRI characterization (mass, edema, eloquent-cortex proximity) is standard of care before neurosurgical tissue acquisition

critical_actions: Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for tissue diagnosis (stereotactic biopsy or maximal safe resection) and operative planning
Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) before any invasive procedure
Administer dexamethasone (loading dose 10 mg IV, then 4 mg IV every 6 hours) to reduce vasogenic edema given imaging evidence of herniation/significant mass effect
Initiate antiepileptic therapy with levetiracetam (preferred non-enzyme-inducing AED) for documented seizure activity
Obtain pre-operative labs (CBC, BMP, coagulation, type & screen) before craniotomy/biopsy
Plan multimodal treatment per molecular and histological profile (e.g., Stupp protocol — concurrent chemoradiation with temozolomide for IDH-wildtype GBM)
Monitor blood glucose closely given anticipated corticosteroid use in a patient with diabetes; adjust antihyperglycemic regimen as needed
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture with herniation risk — herniation risk
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
key_reasoning_points: Combination of progressive headache (worse mornings), new focal neurological deficit, and/or new-onset seizure in an adult is a high-risk presentation requiring urgent contrast-enhanced brain MRI

MRI features of a right hemisphere heterogeneously / ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, perilesional FLAIR-hyperintense edema, restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim, and mass effect are characteristic of high-grade glioma
Perfusion MRI (elevated rCBV) and MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho/NAA, lipid-lactate) corroborate high-grade neoplasm and help guide biopsy targeting
Significant midline shift / herniation risk mandates urgent dexamethasone and neurosurgical evaluation; lumbar puncture is contraindicated
Definitive diagnosis requires tissue (stereotactic biopsy or surgical resection) with molecular profiling (IDH, MGMT, 1p/19q, TERT, H3K27M); imaging alone cannot substitute for histology
For IDH-wildtype GBM, current standard of care is maximal safe resection followed by the Stupp protocol (concurrent radiation + temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide)

Avoid ordering off-pathway advanced-imaging modalities (DaTscan, amyloid PET, FDG-PET, carotid duplex, transcranial Doppler) — they address other neurological differentials and add cost without informing glioma management
New-onset focal or generalized seizure with a focal-onset mass mandates AED therapy (levetiracetam preferred — non-enzyme-inducing, fewer interactions with temozolomide)

key_teaching_points: Classic glioblastoma presentation with progressive headache, focal deficits, and seizure
Importance of comprehensive imaging including perfusion, spectroscopy, and functional MRI
WHO 2021 classification requires molecular profiling for definitive glioma diagnosis
Stupp protocol remains standard of care for newly diagnosed glioblastoma regardless of MGMT status
